label: thmintro:mcg
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmintro:mcg}
Let $S$ be an orientable surface of finite-type, of complexity at least $2$.  The extended mapping class group of $S$, where one allows orientation-reversing homeomorphisms, admits a continuum of equivariant coarse median structures.
head: environment

label: thmintro_coxeter
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmintro_coxeter} 
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite simplicial graph. Suppose that there exist two vertices $v_-, v_+$ such that $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_+\right)=\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_-\right)$ has at least three vertices, is not a join of two proper subgraphs, and is not contained in the link of any other vertex $w\neq v_+,v_-$. Then the right-angled Coxeter group $W_{\Gamma}$ admits a continuum of equivariant coarse median structures.
head: environment

label: thmintro_artin
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thmintro_artin} 
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite simplicial graph. Suppose that there exists a vertex $v\in V(\Gamma)$ such that $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v\right)$ has at least two vertices, is not a join of two proper subgraphs, and is not contained in the link of any other vertex $w\neq v$. Then the right-angled Artin group $A_{\Gamma}$ admits a continuum of equivariant coarse median structures.
head: environment

label: lem:MilnorSchwarz
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:MilnorSchwarz}
    Let $G$ be a group acting $R$-coboundedly on a geodesic metric space $(S,\mathrm{d})$, and let $x_0\in S$ be a point whose orbit is $R$-dense in $S$. Then the set
    \[X\coloneq \{g\in G\mid \mathrm{d}(x_0,gx_0)\le 2R+1\}\]
    generates $G$, and the orbit map $g\to gx_0$ is a $G$-equivariant quasi-isometry $\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)\to S$.
head: environment
name: Milnor-Schwarz

label: defn:1_qc
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:1_qc}
    Let $G$ be a group acting on $\mathbb{R}$ by group automorphisms, and let $\sigma\colon G\to \operatorname{Aut}\left(\mathbb{R}\right)\cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ be the action. A \emph{$\sigma$-quasicocycle} is a map $f\colon G\to \mathbb{R}$ such that there exists a constant $D$, called the \emph{defect} of $f$, such that, for every $g,h\in G$,
    $$|f(g)+\sigma(g)(f(h))-f(gh)|\le D.$$
    A quasicocycle for the trivial action is called a \emph{quasimorphism}. Notice that, if $f$ is a $\sigma$-quasicocycle and $K=\ker(\sigma)$, which has index at most two in $G$, the restriction of $f$ to $K$ is a quasimorphism. 

    A $\sigma$-quasicocycle $f$ is always bounded on the orbit of any $g\in G-K$, because for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ one has
    $$|f(g^{2(2n+1)})|=|f(g^{2(2n+1)})-f(g^{2n+1})+f(g^{2n+1})|\le D.$$
    We say $f$ is \emph{unbounded} if there exists $h\in G$ such that $f|_{\langle h \rangle}$ is unbounded; such a $h$ must necessarily belong to $h$.
head: environment

label: defn:homogeneisation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{defn:homogeneisation}
    A quasimorphism is \emph{homogeneous} if it restricts to a homomorphism on cyclic subgroups. Given any quasimorphism $f\colon K\to \mathbb{R}$ of defect $D$, the limit
    $$\phi(g)=\lim_{n\to+\infty}\frac{f(g^n)}{n}$$
    always exists, and defines a homogeneous quasimorphism of defect at most $2D$ such that $|\phi(g)-f(g)|\le D$ for all $g\in K$ (see e.g. \cite[Lemma 2.21]{calegari}); in particular, a quasimorphism is unbounded if and only if its homogeneisation is non-trivial. Homogeneous quasimorphisms are invariant under conjugation, meaning that $\phi(ghg^{-1})=\phi(h)$ for all $g,h\in K$.
head: environment
name: Homogeneisation

label: ex:busemann
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:busemann}
Let $G$ be a group acting on a \emph{quasiline} $L$, that is, a space which is quasi-isometric to $\mathbb{R}$. The action on $\partial L$ gives a homomorphism $\sigma\colon G\to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, so let $K$ be its kernel. Given a sequence $\{x_n\}\in L$ converging to some $\xi\in \partial L$, the map $\beta_{\{x_n\}}\colon K\to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
  $$\beta_{\{x_n\}}(g)=\limsup_{n\to \infty} \mathrm{d}(gx_0,x_n)-\mathrm{d}(x_0,x_n),$$
is a quasimorphism. Its homogeneisation $\beta$ does not depend on the choice of the sequence, and has the property that an element $g\in K$ acts loxodromically on $L$ if and only if $\beta(g)\neq 0$. Furthermore, \cite[Proposition 2.10]{NL} shows that $\beta$ extends to a $\sigma$-quasicocycle $\phi\colon G\to \mathbb{R}$ by fixing $i\in G-K$ and setting $\phi(ki^n)=\beta(k)$ for every $k\in K$ and $n=0,1$. We stress that the extension is not canonical, though this will not matter for our purposes.
head: environment
name: Busemann quasicocycle

label: lem:quasiline_from_qc
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The main statement is \cite[Lemma 2.14]{NL}. For the ``furthermore" part, \Cref{item:qc1} follows immediately from the fact that $\phi$ is a quasi-isometry. Moving to \Cref{item:qc2}, let $g\in G$, let $k\in K$ such that $\phi|_{\langle k\rangle}$ is unbounded, and suppose without loss of generality that $\lim_{n\to +\infty} \phi(k^n)=+\infty$. Then
    \[\lim_{n\to+\infty} \phi(gk^n)=\lim_{n\to+\infty} \phi(gk^ng^{-1})=\lim_{n\to+\infty} \sigma(g)\psi(k^n)=\sigma(g)\infty,\]
    where for both equalities we used that $f$ is a $\sigma$-quasicocycle. Finally, if $H\le K$ and $\phi|_H$ is bounded, then for every $g\in G$ we also have that $\phi|_{gHg^{-1}}$ is bounded, as $\phi$ is a quasicocycle, and therefore  $\phi|_{gHg^{-1}}\equiv 0$ as $\phi$ restricts to a homogeneous quasimorphism on $K$. Therefore every conjugate of $H$ lies in $X$ by definition of the latter; in turn this proves \Cref{item:qc3}, since \[\mathrm{diam}_{\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)}(H\cdot g)= \mathrm{diam}_{\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)}(g^{-1}H\cdot g)\le 1.\qedhere\]
head: environment

label: cor:quasiline_from_Busemann_qc
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:quasiline_from_Busemann_qc}
    Let $G$ be a group acting on a quasiline $(S,\mathrm{d})$ with a loxodromic element, and let $K$ be the kernel of the action on $\partial S$. Let $\phi\colon G\to \mathbb{R}$ be the Busemann quasicocycle for the action (associated to a choice of element $i\in G-K$), and let $L=\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)$ be the quasiline from \Cref{lem:quasiline_from_qc} induced by $\phi$. Then $L$ and $S$ are $G$-equivariantly quasi-isometric.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L\to S$ be the orbit map $g\to g\cdot x_0$, which is $G$-equivariant by construction and coarsely surjective because $S$ is a quasiline and $G$ contains a loxodromic element. It is therefore enough to show that the orbit map is a quasi-isometry; for the ease of notation, we shall write $A\asymp B$ to mean that there exist constants $K\ge 1,C\ge 0$ such that $B/K-C\le A\le BK+C$.

    We firstly prove that the orbit map restricts to a quasi-isometry on $K$. Recall that the Busemann quasimorphism on $k\in K$ is the homogeneisation of 
    \[\beta_{\{x\}}(k)=\limsup_{n\to+\infty}\mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_n)-\mathrm{d}(x_0,x_n),\]
    where $\{x_n\}_{n\in \mathcal{N}}$ is any sequence converging to a boundary point $\xi$. Notice that for every $n$ one has
    \[\mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_0)\asymp |\mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_n)-\mathrm{d}(x_0, x_n)|\]
    since $S$ is a quasiline. Thus, passing to the limsup or liminf (depending on whether $\beta_{\{x_n\}}(k)$ is positive or negative), we get that
    \[\mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_0)\asymp |\beta_{\{x_n\}}(k)|\asymp |\phi(k)|\asymp |k|_X,\]
    where we used the the definition of $\phi|_K$ as the homogeneisation of $\beta_{\{x_n\}}$, and the fact that $\phi\coloneq \operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)\to \mathbb{R}$ is a quasi-isometry. Now, if $g=ki^n$ for $n\in \{0,1\}$, then the triangle inequality plus the fact that $G$ acts isometrically on $S$ yield
    \[\mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_0) -\mathrm{d}(s\cdot x_0, x_0)\le \mathrm{d}(g\cdot x_0, x_0)\le \mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_0) +\mathrm{d}(i\cdot x_0, x_0),\]
    so
    \[\mathrm{d}(g\cdot x_0, x_0)\asymp \mathrm{d}(k\cdot x_0, x_0)\asymp |k|_X.\]
    In turn, 
    \[|k|_X-|i|_X\le |g|_X\le |k|_X+|i|_X\]
    hence $|k|_X\asymp |g|_X$. This shows that $\mathrm{d}(g\cdot x_0, x_0)\asymp |g|_X$, i.e. the orbit map is a quasi-isometric embedding.

title: Definition
body_md:
A group $G$ is \emph{acylindrically hyperbolic} if it is not virtually cyclic, it acts with unbounded orbits on a Gromov-hyperbolic metric space $(S,\mathrm{d})$, and the action is \emph{acylindrical}, i.e. for every $R\ge 0$ there exist $N>0,L>0$ such that for every $x,y\in S$ with $\mathrm{d}(x,y)\geq L$ one has
    \[\#\{g\in G\mid \mathrm{d}(x,gx)\leq R,\,\mathrm{d} (y,gy)\leq R\}\leq N.\]
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment

label: ex:loxoWPD_is_HH
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:loxoWPD_is_HH} Let $G$ be a non-virtually cyclic group, let $\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)$ be hyperbolic and unbounded, and suppose that the action is acylindrical. Let $g\in G$ act loxodromically on $\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)$, which exists by \cite[Theorem 1.1]{Osin_AH}, and let $E(g)$ be the maximal virtually cyclic subgroup of $G$ containing $g$, which exists by \cite[Lemma 6.5]{DGO}. Then $E(g)\hookrightarrow_h(G,X)$ by \cite[Theorem 6.8]{DGO}, whose proof essentially checks geometric separation. 
    
    For completeness, we point out that the above example can be widely generalised to non-cobounded, non-acylindrical actions as well, provided $g$ satisfies the \emph{WPD property} which, roughly, states that the action is acylindrical ``along the axis of $g$" \cite[Definition 6.1]{DGO}.
head: environment

label: lem:qmorph_from_acylindrical
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:qmorph_from_acylindrical}
Let $G$ be a non-virtually cyclic group, let $X$ be such that $\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)$ is unbounded and hyperbolic, and suppose the $G$-action on $\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)$ is acylindrical. There exists a non-trivial homogeneous quasimorphism $Q\colon G\to \mathbb{R}$ which is coarsely Lipschitz with respect to $X$, meaning that there exists $L\ge 0$ such that, for all $g,h\in G$, $|Q(g)-Q(h)|\le L|gh^{-1}|_X+L$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Claim
body_md: There exists $D\ge 1$ such that, if $g,h\in G$ satisfy $\mathrm{d}_{\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)}(g,h)\le 1$, then the diameter of $\pi_B(g)\cup \pi_B(h)$, with respect to $\mathrm{d}_B$, is at most $D$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: \cite[Lemma 2.8]{FPS} grants the existence of a constant $D\ge 1$ such that, if the diameter of $\pi_B(g)\cup \pi_B(h)$ is at least $D$, then every $\hat G$-geodesic between $g$ and $h$ passes through $c(B)$. If $g=h$ we are done by the Lemma; hence suppose $g$ and $h$ are $X$-adjacent, and therefore $\hat\mathrm{d}(g,h)\le 1$. By the Lemma, if the diameter of their projections was greater than $D$, then the $X$-edge between them would not be a geodesic, so $\hat\mathrm{d}(g,h)$ would have to be $1/2$; as a consequence, the unique geodesic between $g$ and $h$ would have to be the path $\{g,c(B),h\}$, meaning that $g,h$ would belong to $B$. However this is impossible, as then $g=\pi_B(g)$, $h=\pi_B(h)$, and $\mathrm{d}_B(g,h)\le \mathrm{d}_{\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)}(g,h)=1$ as they are $X$-adjacent.
head: environment

label: cor:bounded_orbit_implies_trivial
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:bounded_orbit_implies_trivial}
    In the setting of \Cref{lem:qmorph_from_acylindrical}, if $H\le G$ has a bounded orbit in $\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)$, then $Q|_H\equiv 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\mathrm{diam}_{\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)}(Qg)<T$ for some $g\in G$. By left-invariance of the Cayley metric, $\mathrm{diam}_{\operatorname{Cay}\left(G,X\right)}(g^{-1}Qg)<T$, so for every $h\in Q$ we have that 
    \[Q(h)=Q(g^{-1}hg)\le LT+L.\]
    where we used that $Q$ is homogeneous and therefore invariant under conjugation. But then, again by homogeneity, $Q(h)=\lim_{n\to+\infty}\frac{Q(h^n)}{n}=0$, as required.

label: defn:HHS
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:HHS}
    Let $E>0$, and let $Z $ be an $(E,E)$--quasigeodesic space.  A \emph{hierarchically hyperbolic space (HHS) structure with constant $E$} for $Z $ is an index set $\mathfrak S$ and a set $\{ \mathcal C W \mid W\in\mathfrak S\}$ of $E$-hyperbolic metric spaces $(\mathcal C W,\mathrm{d}_W)$ such that the following axioms are satisfied. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*{})]
        \item\label{axiom:projections} \textbf{(Projections.)} For each $W \in \mathfrak S$, there exists a \emph{projection} $\pi_W \colon Z  \rightarrow 2^{\mathcal C W}$  that is a $(E,E)$--coarsely Lipschitz, $E$--coarsely onto, $E$--coarse map.
	
        \item\label{axiom:nesting} \textbf{(Nesting.)} If $\mathfrak S \neq \emptyset$, then $\mathfrak S$ is equipped with a  partial order $\sqsubseteq$ and contains a unique $\sqsubseteq$--maximal element. When $V\sqsubseteq W$, we say $V$ is \emph{nested} in $W$. For each $W\in\mathfrak S$, we denote by $\mathfrak S_W$ the set of all $V\in\mathfrak S$ with $V\sqsubseteq W$.  Moreover, for all $V,W\in\mathfrak S$ with $V\sqsubsetneq W$ there is a specified non-empty subset $\rho^V_W\subseteq \mathcal C W$ with $\mathrm{diam}(\rho^V_W)\le E$.
            
        \item\label{axiom:finite_complexity}  \textbf{(Finite complexity.)} Any set of pairwise $\sqsubseteq$--comparable elements has cardinality at most $E$.
            
        \item\label{axiom:orthogonal} \textbf{(Orthogonality.)} The set $\mathfrak S$ has a symmetric relation called \emph{orthogonality}. If $V$ and $W$ are orthogonal, we write $V\perp W$ and require that $V$ and $W$ are not $\sqsubseteq$--comparable. Further, whenever $V\sqsubseteq W$ and $W\perp U$, we require that $V\perp U$. We denote by $\mathfrak S_W^\perp$ the set of all $V\in \mathfrak S$ with $V\perp W$.
            
        \item\label{axiom:containers}\textbf{(Containers.)} For each $W \in \mathfrak S$ and $U \in \mathfrak S_W$ with $ \mathfrak S_W\cap \mathfrak S_U^\perp \neq \emptyset$, there exists $Q \in\mathfrak S_W-\{W\}$ such that $V \sqsubseteq Q$ whenever $V \in\mathfrak S_W \cap \mathfrak S_U^\perp$.
		
        \item\label{axiom:transversality} \textbf{(Transversality.)} If $V,W\in\mathfrak S$ are neither orthogonal nor $\sqsubseteq$-comparable, we say $V$ and $W$ are \emph{transverse}, denoted $V\pitchfork W$.  Moreover, for all $V,W \in \mathfrak S$ with $V\pitchfork W$, there are non-empty sets $\rho^V_W\subseteq \mathcal C W$ and $\rho^W_V\subseteq \mathcal C  V$, each of diameter at most $E$.
		
        \item\label{axiom:consistency} \textbf{(Consistency.)} For all $x \in Z $ and $V,W,U \in\mathfrak S$:
	\begin{itemize}
            \item if $V\pitchfork W$, then $\min\left\{\mathrm{d}_{W}(\pi_W(x),\rho^V_W),\mathrm{d}_{V}(\pi_V(x),\rho^W_V)\right\}\le E$, and
            \item if $U\sqsubseteq V$ and either $V\sqsubsetneq W$ or $V\pitchfork W$ and $W\not\perp U$, then $\mathrm{d}_W(\rho^U_W,\rho^V_W)\le E$.
	\end{itemize}
		
        \item\label{axiom:bounded_geodesic_image} \textbf{(Bounded geodesic image.)} For all $V,W\in\mathfrak S$ and for all $x,y \in Z $, if  $V\sqsubsetneq W$ and $\mathrm{d}_V(\pi_V(x),\pi_V(y)) \geq E$, then every $\mathcal C W$--geodesic from $\pi_W(x)$ to $\pi_W(y)$ must intersect $\mathcal{N}_E(\rho_W^V)$.
		
        \item\label{axiom:partial_realisation} \textbf{(Partial realization.)} If $\{V_i\}$ is a finite collection of pairwise orthogonal elements of $\mathfrak S$ and $p_i\in \mathcal C V_i$ for each $i$, then there exists $x\in Z $ so that:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\mathrm{d}_{V_i}(\pi_{V_{i}}(x),p_i)\le E$ for all $i$;
            \item for each $i$ and each $W\in\mathfrak S$, if $V_i\sqsubsetneq W$ or $W\pitchfork V_i$, we have $\mathrm{d}_{W}(\pi_W(x),\rho^{V_i}_W)\le E$.
	\end{itemize}

        \item\label{axiom:uniqueness} \textbf{(Uniqueness.)} There is a function $\theta \colon [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ so that for all $r \geq 0$, if $x,y\in Z $ and $\mathrm{d}_Z (x,y)\geq\theta(r)$, then there exists $W\in\mathfrak S$ such that $\mathrm{d}_W(\pi_W(x),\pi_W(y))\geq r$. 

        \item\label{axiom:large_link_lemma} \textbf{(Large links.)} For all $W\in\mathfrak S$ and  $x,y\in Z $, there exists $\{V_1,\dots,V_m\}\subseteq\mathfrak S_W -\{W\}$ such that $m$ is at most $E \mathrm{d}_{W}(\pi_W(x),\pi_W(y))+E$, and for all $U\in\mathfrak S_W - \{W\}$, either $U\in\mathfrak S_{V_i}$ for some $i$, or $\mathrm{d}_{U}(\pi_U(x),\pi_U(y)) \le E$.  
    \end{enumerate}
    We use $\mathfrak S$ to denote the relative HHS structure, including the index set $\mathfrak S$, spaces $\{\mathcal C W : W \in \mathfrak S\}$, projections $\{\pi_W : W \in \mathfrak S\}$, and relations $\sqsubseteq$, $\perp$, $\pitchfork$.  We call an element $U\in \mathfrak S$ a \emph{domain}, the associated space $\mathcal CU$ its \emph{coordinate space}, and call the maps $\rho_W^V$ the \emph{relative projections} from $V$ to $W$. We say a domain $U$ is \emph{unbounded} if $\mathcal C U$ is unbounded. The number $E$ is called the \emph{hierarchy constant} for $\mathfrak S$; notice that every $E'\ge E$ is again a hierarchy constant for $\mathfrak S$, so we are often free to enlarge $E$ by a bounded amount.  We often suppress reference to the projection maps, so for every $x,y\in Z$ and $U\in \mathfrak S$ we write $\mathrm{d}_U(x,y)$ to mean $\mathrm{d}_U(\pi_U(x), \pi_U(y))$.

label: rem: fi_sgr_is_HHG
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem: fi_sgr_is_HHG}
Notice that, if $G$ is a HHG with underlying HHS $(Z,\mathfrak S)$ and $H$ is a finite-index subgroup of $G$, then $H$ is itself a HHG, with the same underlying HHS.
head: environment

label: rem:BDD
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:BDD}
    Since there are finitely many orbits of domains in a HHG, the latter satisfies the \emph{bounded domain dichotomy}: there exists a constant $C\ge 0$ such that, for every $U\in \mathfrak S$, either $\mathrm{diam}\mathcal C U\le C$ or $U$ is unbounded. When working with a HHG, we therefore can and will assume that the hierarchy constant $E$ is greater than the diameter of any bounded domain.
head: environment
name: Bounded domain dichotomy

label: lem:pairwise_orth_are_at_most_E
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{lem:pairwise_orth_are_at_most_E} If $V_1,\ldots,V_k\in \mathfrak S$ are pairwise orthogonal, then $k\le E$.
head: environment

label: lem:DHS
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:DHS}
    Let $U,V,W\in\mathfrak S$. If $U\bot V$, and both $\rho^U_W$ and $\rho^V_W$ are defined, then $\mathrm{d}_{W}(\rho^U_W,\rho^V_W)\le 2E$.
head: environment

label: lem:acyl_action_on_CS
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{lem:acyl_action_on_CS} A HHG $(G,\mathfrak S)$ acts acylindrically on the top-level coordinate space $\mathcal C S$. As a consequence, if $G$ is not virtually cyclic and $\mathcal C S$ is unbounded, then $G$ is acylindrically hyperbolic.
head: environment

label: defn:CC
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:CC}
    A HHS $(Z,\mathfrak S)$ has \emph{clean containers} if, for every $U\sqsubsetneq V$ $\mathfrak S_V\cap\mathfrak S_U^\bot$ is either empty or it admits a unique maximal element $Q$, called the \emph{orthogonal complement} of $U$ in $V$. If $V=S$, we denote the orthogonal complement of $U$ in $S$ by $U^\bot$.
head: environment
name: Clean containers

label: defn:prodreg
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:prodreg}
Let $\mathcal U=\{U_1,\ldots, U_k\}\subseteq \mathfrak S$ be a collection of pairwise orthogonal domains. For a domain $W\in\mathfrak S$, set $\mathcal U\sqsubsetneq W$ (resp. $\mathcal U\pitchfork W$) if there exists $U_i\in \mathcal U$ such that $U_i\sqsubsetneq W$ (resp. $U_i\pitchfork W$). Then define the \emph{product region} associated to $\mathcal U$ as the subspace
\[P_{\mathcal U}=\left\{x\in Z \mid \mathrm{d}_W\left(x,\bigcup\rho^{U_i}_W\right)\le E\mbox{ whenever } \mathcal U\pitchfork W \mbox{ or }\mathcal U\sqsubsetneq W\right\},\]
where the union is over all $U_i$ for which $\rho^{U_i}_W$ is well-defined. When $\mathcal U$ consists of a single domain $U$, we denote the associated product region simply by $P_U$.

name: Product regions and gates

title: Remark

label: defn:cobounded_pr
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defn:cobounded_pr}
    A HHG has \emph{cobounded product regions} if, for every $U\in\mathfrak S$, $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(U)$ acts coboundedly on $P_U$. In particular, since the whole $G$ acts properly on $Z$, $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(U)$ is quasi-isometric to $P_U$; the gate onto $P_U$ then yields a $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(U)$-equivariant, coarsely Lipschitz coarse retraction $Z\to \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(U)$, which we still call $\mathfrak{g}_U$ with a little abuse of notation.

label: defn:coarse_median
title: Definition
head: environment
name: Coarse median structure

title: Example
body_md: A hyperbolic space $Y$ admits a coarse median structure: for every $a,b,c\in Y$, their coarse median is the coarse centre of any geodesic triangle with these vertices (see e.g. \cite[Proposition III.$\Gamma$.1.17]{bridsonhaefliger}). This coarse median structure is also unique by \cite[Theorem 4.2]{NWZ}.
head: environment
name: Hyperbolic spaces admit coarse median structures

label: ex:coarse_median_from_HHS
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:coarse_median_from_HHS}
By e.g. \cite[Theorem 7.3]{HHS_II}, which in turn builds on an observation of Bowditch \cite{bowditch_mcg}, a HHS $(Z,\mathfrak S)$ admits a coarse median structure $\mu$, obtained as follows: for every $x,y,z\in Z$ and every $U\in\mathfrak S$, the $U$-coordinate of $\mu(x,y,z)$ coarsely agrees with the coarse median of $\pi_U(x),\pi_U(y),\pi_U(z)$ in the hyperbolic space $\mathcal C U$. In other words, the coarse median associated to $(Z,\mathfrak S)$ makes all coordinate projections $\pi_U\colon Z\to \mathcal C U$ coarse median preserving, and is characterised by this property by the uniqueness axiom \Cref{defn:HHS}.\eqref{axiom:uniqueness}; as we will prove in \Cref{thm:uncountably_many_CM}, different HHS structures can produce different coarse median structures. Notice also that, if $(Z,\mathfrak S)$ is a HHG structure for a group $G$, then $\mu$ is $G$-equivariant, by how $G$ acts on coordinate spaces.
head: environment
name: HHSs admit coarse median structures

title: Definition
body_md: Let $(Z,\mathrm{d}, \mu)$ be a coarse median space. A subset $Y\subseteq Z$ is \emph{median-quasiconvex}, or quasiconvex with respect to $\mu$, if there exists a constant $K\ge 0$ such that, for every $y,y'\in Y$ and $z\in Z$, $\mu(y,y',z)\in N_R(Y)$. If $(G,\mu)$ is a coarse median group and $Z$ is a Cayley graph for $G$ with respect to a finite generating set, we say that a finitely generated subgroup $H$ is median-quasiconvex if the orbit $H\cdot g\subseteq Z$ is median-quasiconvex, for some choice of $g\in G$ (hence every choice, by e.g. \cite[Lemma 2.3(6)]{FS_pantsgraph}).
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: A median-quasiconvex subset inherits a well-defined coarse median structure. In the case of a median-quasiconvex subgroup, the inherited coarse median structure is equivariant.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $Y\subseteq Z$ be $K$-quasiconvex with respect to $\mu$. For all $y_1,y_2,y_3\in Y$, define $\mu_Y(y_1,y_2,y_3)$ as any point in $Y$ within distance $K$ from $\mu(y_1,y_2,y_3)$. We can assume that $\mu_Y\coloneq Y^3\to Y$ is symmetric, and that if $y_1=y_2$ then $\mu_Y(y_1,y_1,y_3)=y_1=\mu(y_1,y_1,y_3)$; in the case where $Y$ is a subgroup of a coarse median group, one can also choose $\mu_Y$ to be coarsely equivariant with respect to the $Y$-action. Any two possible choices for $\mu_Y(y_1,y_2,y_3)$ are at distance at most $2K$, so $\mu_Y$ is coarsely well-defined. Moreover, $\mu_Y$ is a coarse median on $(Y,\mathrm{d})$. Indeed, we chose $\mu_Y$ to satisfy symmetry and localisation; the coarsely Lipschitz property was already satisfied by $\mu$; and coarse associativity is a combination of the coarsely Lipschitz property and coarse associativity for $\mu$.

label: construction:newline
title: Construction
body_md:
\label{construction:newline} Firstly, by \Cref{lem:MilnorSchwarz}, we once and for all replace $Z$ by a Cayley graph for $G$, with respect to some finite generating set. Next, since $(G,\mathfrak S)$ has cobounded product regions, $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)$ acts coboundedly on $\mathcal C \ell^\bot$, so $H$ acts coboundedly on $\mathcal C \ell^\bot/\langle T\rangle$. By the Milnor-Schwarz \Cref{lem:MilnorSchwarz}, there exists a generating set $X_0$ for $H$ such that $\operatorname{Cay}\left(H,X_0\right)$ is equivariantly quasi-isometric to $\mathcal C \ell^\bot/\langle T\rangle$. Then the set $X\coloneq X_0\cap \{T^k\}_{k\neq 0}$ generates $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)$ and $\operatorname{Cay}\left(\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell),X\right)$ is equivariantly quasi-isometric to $\mathcal C \ell^\bot/\langle T\rangle$, and therefore to $\mathcal C \ell^\bot$ since $\langle T\rangle$ acts on it with uniformly bounded orbits. We therefore once and for all replace every $G$-translate of $\mathcal C \ell^\bot$ by the corresponding translate of $\operatorname{Cay}\left(\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell),X\right)$ in the HHG structure.
    
    By \Cref{lem:qmorph_from_acylindrical}, there exists a non-trivial homogeneous quasimorphism $Q\colon H\to \mathbb{R}$ which is $X_0$-coarsely Lipschitz; in turn, if we denote by $p_\ell$ the projection $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)\to H$, the composition $\psi\coloneq \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)\xrightarrow{p_\ell} H \xrightarrow{Q} \mathbb{R} $ is a non-trivial homogeneous quasimorphism which is $X$-coarsely-Lipschitz. 
    
    Now let $\sigma\colon \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)\to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ be the action on the ideal endpoints of $\mathcal C \ell$, with kernel $K$. Let $\phi\colon \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)\to \mathbb{R}$ be the Busemann quasicocycle for the action on $\mathcal C \ell$, as in \Cref{ex:busemann}; in the case where $K\lneq \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)$, the latter depends on the choice of some element $i\in \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)-K$. By \Cref{cor:quasiline_from_Busemann_qc}, up to equivariantly replacing $\mathcal C \ell$ and its translates in $(G,\mathfrak S)$, we can assume that it coincides with the quasiline produced by \Cref{lem:quasiline_from_qc}, and therefore that $\phi\colon \mathcal C\ell\to \mathbb{R}$ is a quasi-isometry.
    
    For every $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ consider the linear combination
    \[\theta_\lambda\coloneq\phi+\lambda\psi\colon \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)\to \mathbb{R}\]
    which is again a $\sigma$-quasicocycle; notice that $\theta_\lambda(T)=\phi(T)\neq 0$, so $\theta_\lambda$ is unbounded. \Cref{lem:quasiline_from_qc} then produces a generating set $S_\lambda$ for $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)$ such that $L_\lambda\coloneq \operatorname{Cay}\left(\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell),S_\lambda\right)$ is a quasiline and $\theta_\lambda\colon L_\lambda\to \mathbb{R}$ is a quasi-isometry.

body_md:

            $\langle T\rangle$ acts loxodromically on $L_\lambda$ and with uniformly bounded orbits on $\mathcal C W$ whenever $W\in \mathfrak S_\lambda$ is orthogonal to $\ell$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Since $\theta_\lambda(T)=\phi(T)\neq 0$, $\langle T\rangle$ still acts loxodromically on $L_\lambda$. If $W\bot\ell$ is not in the $G$-orbit of $\ell$, then $\langle T\rangle$ already acted with uniformly bounded orbits on $\mathcal C W$ by \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:dehntwist}, so there is nothing to prove. If instead $\ell\bot g\ell$ for some $g\in G$, by symmetry it is enough to show that $gTg^{-1}$ acts with uniformly bounded orbits on $L_\lambda$. Recall that $gTg^{-1}$ fixes by $\ell$ \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:dehntwist}, so it belongs to $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)$; moreover, again by assumption, $g\langle T\rangle g^{-1}$ acts with uniformly bounded orbits on the original $\mathcal C\ell$, so it must commute with $T$ which acts loxodromically. Thus $gTg^{-1}$ belongs to the kernel of the $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)$-action on $L_\lambda$. By \Cref{lem:quasiline_from_qc}.\eqref{item:qc3}, we are therefore left to prove that $\theta_\lambda(gTg^{-1})=0$. This is because $\phi(gTg^{-1})=0$ (here we are using that $\phi$ is the Busemann quasicocycle for the action on $\mathcal C \ell$); moreover, $\psi(gTg^{-1})=0$ by \Cref{cor:bounded_orbit_implies_trivial}, since $gTg^{-1}$ fixes the bounded subset $\rho^{g\ell}_{\ell^\bot}\subset \mathcal C \ell^\bot$.

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we assume that $S$ has no boundary components, and check that $\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$ satisfies the requirements of \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}. By results of many authors \cite{MM1, MM2, Behrstock, BKMM, HHS_I}, $\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$ is hierarchically hyperbolic; here we shall use the explicit HHG structure from \cite[Theorem 9.8]{converse}, where:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\mathfrak S$ is the collection of isotopy classes of subsurfaces whose connected components are not pairs of pants. The precise definition of the word ``subsurface" is a bit subtle (see \cite[Section 9.1]{converse}), but we won't need to go into details here. 
    \item Nesting and orthogonality respectively correspond to subsurface inclusion and disjointness, up to isotopy (with some little caveats, again see \cite[Section 9.1]{converse}).
    \item For every subsurface $U\in\mathfrak S$ which is not an annulus, $\mathcal C U$ is the \emph{curve graph} of $U$, that is, the simplicial graph whose vertices are isotopy classes of simple closed curve on $U$ and edges connect curves with the minimal intersection number; if $U$ has complexity at least $2$, this is equivalent to connecting two curves if they are disjoint. If $U\in \mathfrak S$ is an annulus, $\mathcal C U$ is the \emph{annular curve graph} from \cite[Section 2.4]{MM2}, which is a quasiline on which the Dehn twist along $U$ acts loxodromically. 
\end{itemize}
As proven in \cite[Theorem 9.8]{converse}, $(Z,\mathfrak S)$ has clean containers. Furthermore, the structure has cobounded product regions: this is essentially because the stabiliser of a subsurface $U$ is virtually the product of the mapping class groups of the mapping class groups of the connected components of $U$ and $S-U$. We therefore checked \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:prodregions}.

Now, if $S$ has genus at least $1$, let $\ell$ be a non-separating curve; if instead $S$ is a sphere let $\ell$ be a curve cutting out a pair of pants. Notice that $\ell$ is $\sqsubseteq$-minimal and its annular curve graph is a quasiline, so \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:annular_curve_graph} holds. If $S$ has genus at least $1$, the orthogonal complement $\ell^\bot$ is precisely the subsurface $S-\ell$, which has complexity at least one by the assumption on the complexity of $S$ and therefore is not a pair of pants or an annulus; if instead $S$ is a sphere, $\ell^\bot$ is the connected component of $S-\ell$ which is not a pair of pants, which exists again by the assumption on the complexity of $S$. In both cases, $\ell^\bot$ is an open, connected subsurface of complexity at least $1$, so its curve graph is unbounded by \cite[Theorem 1.1]{MM1}. Moving to the second requirement of \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:orth_compl}, if $S$ has genus at least one then $S$ is the unique subsurface containing $\ell^\bot$, while in the case of a punctured sphere the only non-maximal subsurface containing $\ell^\bot$ is its closure, which contains $\ell$ as its boundary and therefore has bounded curve graph. Next, the orthogonal complement of $\ell^\bot$ is $\ell$ itself (in the sphere case, we are using that pair of pants do not belong to the index set). Finally, every subsurface which is transverse to $\ell$ is also transverse to $\ell^\bot$, as $\ell$ is the boundary of the closure of $\ell^\bot$. Hence \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:orth_compl} is proven.

Finally, let $T$ be the (right) Dehn twist around $\ell$, which is normal in $\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)}(\ell)$ because a mapping class $f\in \mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$ conjugates $\langle T\rangle$ to the subgroup generated by the Dehn Twist on $f(\ell)$. Notice that $T$ acts loxodromically on the annular curve graph for $\ell$, it fixes every subsurface $U$ which is disjoint from $\ell$, and it acts with uniformly bounded orbits on $\mathcal C U$ by \cite[Lemma 2.3]{MM2}; this proves  \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:dehntwist}. Regarding \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:acylindricity} , by e.g. \cite[Proposition 3.19]{FarbMargalit} the quotient $H=\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\ell)/\langle T\rangle$ is virtually the mapping class group of $\ell^\bot$, which is not virtually cyclic by the assumption on the complexity and acts acylindrically on $\mathcal C \ell^\bot$ by e.g. \cite{Bowditch_tight}.


We finally turn to the case where $S=S^b_{g,p}$ with $b> 0$. Again by e.g. \cite[Proposition 3.19]{FarbMargalit}, there exists a central extension
	\[0\to \mathbb{Z}^b\to \mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)\xrightarrow{q} \mathcal M(S')\to 0,\]
	where $S'$ is obtained from $S$ by gluing a once-punctured disk to each boundary component and $\mathcal M(S')$ is a finite-index subgroup of $\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S')$; notice in particular that, by \Cref{rem: fi_sgr_is_HHG}, $\mathcal M(S')$ inherits a continuum of HHG structures $(\mathcal M(S'),\mathfrak S_\lambda)$ whose associated equivariant coarse median structure are all different. By combining  e.g. \cite[Proposition 6.4]{Fujiwara-Kapovich} and \cite[Theorem 3.12]{FournierFacioMangioniSisto_bcohom_HHG2026}, $\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$ has a HHG structure whose coordinate projections are either certain quasilines for the centre, or are obtained by composing the $1$-Lipschitz projection $q\colon \mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)\to\mathcal M(S')$ with the coordinate projections for $\mathcal M(S')$. In particular, by \Cref{ex:coarse_median_from_HHS}, for every $x,y,z\in \mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$ and every HHS structure for $\mathcal M(S')$, the $q$-projection of the coarse median of $x,y,z$ in $\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$ is precisely the coarse median of $q(x),q(y),q(z)$ in $\mathcal M(S')$. In turn, since $q$ is $1$-Lipschitz, the continuum of HHG structures for $\mathcal M(S')$ produces a continuum of equivariant coarse median structures for $\mathcal{MCG}^\pm(S)$, as required.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Sigma_\Gamma$ be the Davis complex for $W_\Gamma$. We first describe the HHG structure $(\Sigma_\Gamma,\mathfrak S)$ on $W_{\Gamma}$ constructed in \cite[Proposition 8.3]{HHS_I}. The latter is stated for a right-angled Artin group acting on the universal cover of the Salvetti complex  but its proof works also for a right-angled Coxeter group acting on its Davis complex, with minor adjustments due to the fact that the vertex set of $\Sigma_\Gamma$ is not in bijection with $W_{\Gamma}$. For simplicity, whenever possible, we shall also reformulate the structure directly in terms of $\Gamma$ and $W_\Gamma$, without referencing the underlying cubical structure, as in e.g. \cite[page 8]{quasiflats}.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the collection of full subgraphs of $\Gamma$ with the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Gamma\in \mathcal F$;
\item If $\emptyset\subsetneq \Delta\subseteq \operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(w\right)$ for some $w\in V(\Gamma)$, and $\Delta$ either contains both $v_+$ and $v_-$ or none of them, then $\Delta\in \mathcal F$.
\end{itemize} 
Notice that $\mathcal F$ contains all links of vertices, since by assumption $v_+$ belongs to some $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(w\right)$ if and only if $v_-$ does. Moreover, whenever $\Lambda,\Delta\in\mathcal F$ have non-empty intersection, then $\Lambda\cap\Delta\in \mathcal F$. Hence $\mathcal F$ satisfies the requirement of \cite[Proposition 8.3]{HHS_I}, and therefore induces the following HHG structure on $W_\Gamma$. 

For a full subgraph $\Lambda\subseteq \Gamma$, let $W_\Lambda$ be the parabolic subgroup generated by the vertices of $\Lambda$. Let $\mathfrak S=\{gW_\Lambda\}_{\sim}$, where $\Lambda\in \mathcal F$, $g\in W_{\Gamma}$, and $\sim$ is the equivalence relation $gW_\Lambda\sim hW_\Lambda$ if $gh^{-1}$ centralises $W_\Lambda$. Declare $[gW_\Lambda]\sqsubseteq[gW_{\Lambda'}]$ if $\Lambda\subseteq \Lambda'$, and $[gW_\Lambda]\bot[gW_{\Lambda'}]$ if $\Lambda\subseteq\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(\Lambda'\right)$. For every $F\in \mathfrak S$, the associated coordinate space is its \emph{factored contact graph}. We defer its definition to \cite[Definition 8.14]{HHS_I}; the only properties we will need are that:
\begin{itemize}
\item If $\Lambda\in \mathcal F$ is neither a vertex nor a proper join, then $\mathcal C [W_\Lambda]$ is unbounded. 
\item If $\{a,b\}\in \mathcal F$ are two non-adjacent vertices, then $\mathcal C [W_{\{a,b\}}]$ is a quasiline, on which the dihedral subgroup $W_{\{a,b\}}$ acts geometrically.
\end{itemize}
The coarse median structure induced by $(\Sigma_\Gamma,\mathfrak S)$, as in \Cref{ex:coarse_median_from_HHS}, is precisely the cubical one; this follows e.g. from the arguments in \cite[Sections 22 and 23]{CRHK}.

We now check the requirements of \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}. Clean containers is immediate: if $\Lambda\subsetneq\Lambda'$ and both belong to $\mathcal F$, the container for $[gW_\Lambda]$ in $[gW_{\Lambda'}]$ is $[gW_{\Delta}]$, where $\Delta=\Lambda'\cap\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(\Lambda\right)\in \mathcal F$ (unless $\Delta$ is trivial, and therefore $[gW_\Lambda]$ is orthogonal to no domain in $[gW_{\Lambda'}]$). Furthermore, the product region associated to $[gW_\Lambda]$ is precisely the Davis complex for $W_{\operatorname{Star}_{\Gamma}\left(\Lambda\right)}=\operatorname{Stab}_{W_{\Gamma}}([gW_\Lambda])$, on which the latter acts cocompactly; hence \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:prodregions} is proven.

Now let $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)\coloneq \operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_+\right)=\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_-\right)=\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(\{v_+,v_-\}\right)$, and let
$\ell=[\{v_+,v_-\}]$; the latter is indeed an element of $\mathfrak S$ since $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)$ is non-empty, so there is some $w\in V(\Gamma)$ whose link contains $\{v_+,v_-\}$. Towards proving \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:annular_curve_graph}, $[W_{\{v_=,v_-\}}]$ is $\sqsubseteq$-minimal because neither $\{v^+\}$ nor $\{v^-\}$ belong to $\mathcal F$; furthermore $v_+$ and $v_-$ are not adjacent since $v_+\not\in\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_+\right)=\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)$, so as mentioned above $\mathcal C \ell$ is a quasiline. 

Moving to \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:orth_compl}, the orthogonal complement of $\ell$ is $\ell^\bot=[W_{\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)}]$. Notice that $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v\right)$ is neither a vertex nor a proper join, so $\mathcal C \ell^\bot$ is unbounded. Notice also that $\ell^\bot$ is only nested in $[W_{\Gamma}]$, since no other link of a vertex contains $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)$; for the same reason $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)\right)=\{v_+,v_-\}$, so $(\ell^\bot)^\bot=\ell$. In turn, the two properties combined imply that any $W\pitchfork \ell$ must also be transverse to $\ell^\bot$. Indeed, $W\not\sqsubseteq \ell^\bot$ or it would be orthogonal to $\ell$, $\ell^\bot\not\sqsubsetneq W$ or $W$ would coincide with $[W_{\Gamma}]$, and $W\not\bot \ell^\bot$ or it would lie inside $(\ell^\bot)^\bot=\ell$. This proves \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:orth_compl}.

Next, let $T=v_+v_-\in W_{\Gamma}$, which is normal in $\operatorname{Stab}_{W_{\Gamma}}(\ell)=\langle v_+,v_-\rangle\times W_{\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)}$. Notice that $T$ acts loxodromically on $\mathcal C\ell$, it fixes all domains nested inside $W_{\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)}$ by how we defined the index set, and acts trivially on the associated coordinate spaces, so \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:dehntwist} holds. Finally, $\operatorname{Stab}_{W_{\Gamma}}(\ell)/\langle T\rangle$ is an index-two overgroup of $W_{\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)}$, which is not virtually cyclic because $\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)$ is neither a simplex nor the suspension of a (possibly empty) simplex; moreover, it acts acylindrically on $\mathcal C\ell^\bot/\langle T\rangle=\mathcal C\ell^\bot$ because $(W_{\operatorname{Link}_{\Gamma}\left(v_\pm\right)},\mathfrak S_{\ell^\bot})$ is itself a HHG, and therefore we can apply \Cref{lem:acyl_action_on_CS}. This proves \Cref{notation:tweakable_hhg}.\eqref{need:acylindricity}, and concludes the proof of \Cref{thmintro_coxeter}.

label: cor:new_median_is_the_same_on_DT_RACG
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{cor:new_median_is_the_same_on_DT_RACG} Let $H$ be a product of Dihedral parabolic subgroups, and for all $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}$ let $\mu_\lambda$ be the coarse median induced by $(\Sigma_\Gamma,\mathfrak S_\lambda)$. Then $H$ is $\mu_\lambda$-quasiconvex, and the restriction of $\mu_\lambda$ to $H$ is equivalent to the standard cubical coarse median.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\{v_i,w_i\}_{i=1,\ldots, k}$ be a collection of pairs of disjoint vertices spanning a join in $\Gamma$, let $D_i=W_{\{v_i,w_i\}}$, $\mathcal U=\{[D_i]\}\subseteq \mathfrak S$, and let $H=\prod_{i=1}^k D_i$. Our goal is to prove that 
\[ \sup_{a,b,c\in H}\mathrm{d}_{W_{\Gamma}}(\mu(a,b,c), \mu_\lambda(a,b,c))<+\infty,\]
where $\mu=\mu_0$ is the standard cubical coarse median, induced by the original HHG structure $(\Sigma_\Gamma,\mathfrak S)$. By the uniqueness axiom in $(\Sigma_\Gamma,\mathfrak S_\lambda)$, it will be enough to show that $m\coloneq \mu(a,b,c)$ and $m_\lambda\coloneq \mu_\lambda(a,b,c)$ project uniformly close to each $W\in\mathfrak S_\lambda$.

Notice that, in both HHG structures, $H$ acts geometrically on the product region for $\mathcal U$, defined as in \Cref{defn:prodreg}. This is because the only domains in $\mathfrak S_\lambda$ (resp. $\mathfrak S$) where the projection of $H$ is not uniformly bounded are the elements of $\mathcal U$, and each $D_i$ acts geometrically on the associated quasiline and with uniformly bounded orbits on the others (if some $U_i$ is a translate of $\ell$, we are using that $T$ acts loxodromically on $L_\lambda$ and trivially on its translates, by the ``furthermore" part of \Cref{prop:new_hhg_structures}). Notice also that $P_{\mathcal U}$ is median-quasiconvex, by how the coarse median is constructed in \Cref{ex:coarse_median_from_HHS}. Thus, up to modifying both coarse median structures by a uniformly bounded amount, we can assume that $m,m_\lambda\in H$. 

Hence we are left to show that $m$ and $m_\lambda$ project uniformly close to all elements of $\mathcal U$. If $[D_i]\not \in W_\Gamma\cdot \ell$, then the projection $\pi_{[D_i]}$ is the same as in the original structure, and therefore $\pi_{[D_i]}(m)=\pi_{[D_i]}(m_\lambda)$. Suppose instead that $[D_i]=g \ell$ for some $g\in W_\Gamma$, and notice that we can choose $g=1$ as $\ell$ is the equivalence class of a standard Dihedral subgroup. Notice that $H\le \operatorname{Stab}_{W_\Gamma}(\ell)$, and that the quasimorphism $\psi\colon \operatorname{Stab}_{W_\Gamma}(\ell)\to \mathbb{R}$ from \Cref{construction:newline} is trivial on $H$ by \Cref{cor:bounded_orbit_implies_trivial}, so $\theta_0|_H\equiv \theta_\lambda|_H=\phi_H$. In particular, if without loss of generality $\phi(a)\le \phi(b)\le\phi(c)$, then the projection of $m$ to $\mathcal C \ell$ (resp. $m_\lambda$ to $L_\lambda$) uniformly coarsely coincides with the projection of $b$. Finally, since $m\in H$, we also have that $\pi_{\mathcal C\ell^\bot}(m)$ and $\pi_{\mathcal C\ell^\bot}(b)$ coarsely coincide; hence \Cref{claim:what_determines_pilambda} implies that $\pi_{L_\lambda}(m)$ coarsely coincides with $\pi_{L_\lambda}(b)$, which in turn coarsely coincides with $\pi_{L_\lambda}(m_\lambda)$.
